implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: range adaptors are applied to views lazily and compose into pipelines whose actions take place as the view is iterated, so a chain of filter/transform/take produces no intermediate container and the algorithm at the end drives the single pass. Views are lightweight, copyable in constant time and can be returned or passed around as one expression, which keeps the pipeline readable where a hand loop used to be needed.
pitfalls: A view is not a container: storing it can dangle when the underlying range dies, and every iteration re-evaluates the whole chain unless you materialize.
Adaptors that need a common range (or differ in const-iterability) change the pipeline's type; use views::common or materialize when interfacing with pre-C++20 APIs.
Stateful projections inside views are re-run on every iteration and can change results; keep adaptor closures pure.

variants.name: range-v3 views pipeline (pre-C++20 library)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++20 route: range-v3 provides the same composable adaptations where the adaptation happens lazily as the view is iterated, plus eager actions that mutate a container in place, for toolchains that stop at C++14/C++17 or need adaptors that only range-v3 ships. Use it as a migration layer: the pipeline syntax mirrors std::views, so moving to <ranges> later is mostly a namespace change.
pitfalls: Two view vocabularies in one codebase (std::views and ranges::views) invite conversion mistakes; pick one per module boundary.
range-v3 is header-only, so compile times and binary size grow; the views still dangle if the underlying range dies.

variants.name: Expression templates / lazy arithmetic (numeric libraries)
variants.implementation_notes: For arithmetic chains the classic C++ fusion is expression templates: operators build a compile-time expression tree and the assignment evaluates it element-wise in one pass with no temporary per operand. Eigen documents exactly this - compile-time mechanisms enable lazy evaluation and remove temporaries, with eval()/noalias() as the manual overrides. Choose it when the data are numeric arrays and the pipeline is arithmetic rather than record-shaped; the mechanism is provided by the library, not written per project.
pitfalls: Aliasing: an expression assigned onto a buffer it reads needs explicit evaluation (eval()/noalias()) or the result is wrong.
Expression templates carry compile-time cost and unreadable type names in diagnostics; keep them out of public interfaces.
Fusing a chain of tiny arithmetic operations can still lose to a tuned BLAS/vectorized kernel; measure.
